confidence_note: Stevenson details come from Gallo's own pieces (Entrepreneur excerpt and HBR article) which accompany the book; his two accounts split the non-story third differently, so only the 65 percent story share is used. Brain coupling is as Gallo reports it, no study details. The old pure-data vs story imaging experiment was dropped.
facts: Stevenson's 2013 TED talk, 'We need to talk about an injustice', ran 18 minutes and was built from three personal stories; he opened with one about his grandmother, 'because everyone has a grandmother'.
Stevenson is a civil rights attorney who argues before the U.S. Supreme Court and won Miller v. Alabama (no mandatory life without parole for juveniles convicted of murder).
The stories supported one theme: young people in underserved communities who grow up without a sense of identity and make seriously bad decisions.
Gallo counts about 65 percent of the talk as stories; accounts of the remainder differ (data 10 percent in one, logic 25 and credibility 10 in another).
Gallo reports the longest standing ovation in TED history and about one million dollars donated by audience members to the Equal Justice Initiative.

Gallo: when someone tells another a story, the same regions of their brains are engaged; researchers call it brain-to-brain coupling, he calls it a mind meld; stories activate language, sensory, visual and motor areas.
Gallo says workplace talks lean heavily on data and rarely on stories.
scene_details: The grandmother story that opened the talk: 'because everyone has a grandmother'.
Three personal stories in eighteen minutes.
tension: A talk heavy on a hard subject opened with stories, not numbers.
opening_idea: Start with the five minutes before the first statistic.

lessons.idea: Lead with a person, then give the figure.
lessons.anchor: Stevenson's three stories before his first statistic.
